title: Emotional patterns over time
keyIdea: An emotional pattern is when the same trigger brings the same feeling and the same response again and again. A one-off is not a pattern. Split each moment into a chain: trigger, feeling, response. Your body gives early warning signs, and a coping plan works best when those signs are still small. Feelings like nerves do not vanish as you grow, but your emotional awareness and your responses can get wiser, and a useful goal says when you will notice and what you will do.

kid: A pattern is something that keeps happening. Maybe you feel worried before every test, or grumpy every time you are hungry. When the same thing sets off the same feeling again and again, that is an emotional pattern.

The thing that sets a feeling off is called a trigger. The feeling is what goes on inside you. The response is what you say or do. So a chain might be: test, then worried, then saying you feel sick. Once you know your chain, you can change the last link.

Feelings often grow bit by bit. Your body gives early warning signs, like a tight tummy, hot cheeks or fast breathing. If you notice the sign when it is small, a calming plan works much better than when the feeling is huge.

One bad day is not a pattern. And the aim is not to never feel worried or cross. Those feelings are normal. The aim is to know your own patterns, to see how you handle them better than when you were little, and to set a goal like this: When my tummy goes tight before a test, I will take five slow breaths.
adult: This topic is part of self-awareness, the first CASEL skill. In England, the Relationships Education guidance asks pupils to recognise and talk about their feelings. It also asks them to judge whether what they feel and do is in proportion. The IB PYP strand on identity asks pupils of this age to look back at how their grasp of feelings has changed.

The core skill is to reflect over time. Children track a trigger that keeps coming back. They name the feeling, describe their usual response and look for early warning signs in the body. A two-week feelings diary shows repeats that a child cannot see from one day.

Common mistakes: calling one upsetting event a pattern; mixing up the feeling and the response, as in saying that shouting is a feeling; waiting until a feeling is huge before trying to cope; thinking that growing up should make nerves or anger go away; and setting vague goals, such as be better or never get angry, that name no trigger and no action.

Good goals take a when-then form: when I notice a sign, I will do my plan. Research calls these if-then plans, and they make a new response more likely in the moment. Ask your child how they handled a trigger at five and how they handle it now. Praise the change they can name.

familyTip: Keep a two-week feelings diary on the fridge: one line a day for what happened, the feeling and what your child did. On Sunday, look together for any trigger that came up twice, and write one When I notice…, I will… goal for it.

visual.caption: Is it a pattern or a one-off? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Grumpy each day I come home hungry
Cross whenever I lose a board game
Sad on the day my goldfish died
Scared once when a big dog barked
Excited on my birthday trip to the zoo

lab.caption: Flagship lab: spot repeats in a feelings diary, build trigger-feeling-response chains, flag the first warning sign, match then and now, and sort useful goals.

practice.prompt: Leo felt worried before {n} out of {n} spelling tests this term. What is this?
choices: A pattern: the same trigger brings the same feeling
practice.hint: Did it happen once, or again and again with the same trigger?
practice.explain: Worry came before all {n} tests. The same trigger bringing the same feeling again and again is a pattern.

practice.prompt: "My sister reads my diary. I feel furious. I slam my door." Which part is the response?
practice.hint: The response is what you say or do that other people can see.
practice.explain: Slamming the door is what you do, so it is the response. Furious is the feeling, and the sister reading the diary is the trigger.

practice.prompt: Worry builds from 2 to 10 out of 10 on the night before a test. It is now at {n} of 10 and your tummy feels a bit tight. When should you use your calming plan?
choices: Now, while the sign is small
Never, it will pass by itself
practice.hint: Is a feeling easier to calm when it is small or when it is huge?
practice.explain: At {n} of 10 the worry is still small, and a tight tummy is an early warning sign. A calming plan works best now.

practice.prompt: Which goal is the most useful?
choices: When I feel my cheeks go hot, I will walk away and count to ten
practice.hint: A useful goal says when you will notice something and what you will do.
practice.explain: It names the sign to notice (hot cheeks) and the plan (walk away and count). Never getting angry is not possible, and be better is too vague.

choices: The thing that happens and sets a feeling off
What you do after the feeling
pool.hint: In the chain trigger, feeling, response, which link comes first?
pool.explain: A trigger is the event that sets a feeling off, like a test or losing a game. The feeling and the response come after it.

pool.prompt: Mia felt shy on the first day at a new club, but fine for the next {n} weeks. Is the shy feeling a pattern?
pool.hint: A pattern keeps coming back. Did the shy feeling repeat?
pool.explain: She was shy once and then fine for {n} weeks. A feeling that happens once is a one-off, not a pattern.

pool.prompt: Which of these is an early warning sign of worry?
pool.hint: Early warning signs are clues in your body.
pool.explain: A tight tummy is a body clue that worry is starting. Noticing it early gives you time to use a plan.

pool.prompt: At age 5, Sam cried when he lost a game. Now he is 10. Which shows his emotional awareness has grown?
choices: He feels let down, says good game and asks for a rematch
He never feels let down now
He hides the game so nobody can play
pool.hint: Growing up does not mean the feeling vanishes. Look for a wiser response.
pool.explain: He still feels let down, which is normal, but now he names it and responds in a better way. That is growth.

pool.prompt: Tom felt grumpy on {n} school mornings after going to bed late. What should he notice first?
choices: That he is a grumpy person
pool.hint: What came before the grumpy feeling each time?
pool.explain: On all {n} mornings the grumpy feeling followed a late night. Spotting that trigger is the first step to changing the pattern.

pool.prompt: Ali feels nervous before swimming. Bea feels excited. What is true?
choices: People can have different emotional patterns
Bea is not telling the truth
pool.hint: Can the same event bring different feelings in different people?
pool.explain: No feeling is wrong. Different people have different triggers and patterns, so knowing your own matters.

pool.prompt: What does a feelings diary help you do?
choices: See repeats that you cannot see from one day
Make sure you are never upset
pool.hint: Think about what you can see when you look back over two weeks.
pool.explain: Writing one line a day lets you look back and spot a trigger that keeps bringing the same feeling.
